title: STEALER OF SOULS: Can Notebook LM really replace podcasts?
description: Send us Fan Mail Can AI truly capture the essence of a podcast, or are we sacrificing the soul of storytelling for convenience? In a very special (and shorter than usual) episode we put Google's LM Notebook to the test, an AI tool that promises to transform text and audio into engaging podcast episodes. By feeding it the transcripts of our popular episodes "Energy and AI" and "Artificial Appetite," we created condensed AI generated podcast coversation. So you can get to see firsthand if AI can match the richness of human-hosted content. This experiment isn't just about technology; it's a call for you to weigh in on whether AI can genuinely replicate the magic of traditional podcasting. Of course AI could never replace Matt & Jimmy. Could it?
summary: A solo Matt experiments with Google's NotebookLM, feeding it transcripts of two past episodes — the Anders Hove energy interview and Artificial Appetite — and playing the AI-generated podcast versions back to back with the originals. The result is a thoughtful test of whether AI-summarized podcasts are engaging or, as Matt concedes, a bit boring and vanilla.
keyTalkingPoints: NotebookLM ingests PDFs, text and audio, then generates a two-host conversational podcast summarizing the material
The AI versions condensed a 50-minute energy episode and an 80-minute society episode into tight, listenable dialogues
Matt's verdict: impressive as a workplace training and summarization tool, but lacking charisma — vanilla rather than a threat to human podcasts
The AI hosts wove in citations and nuance (greenwashing critiques, AGI caveats) fairly faithfully to the source episodes
The episode doubles as an implicit bet on the show's moat: reactive banter, running jokes and genuine disagreement are hard to synthesize

matt: NotebookLM is a really cool summarization tool, especially for workplace training, but the generated podcasts sound boring and vanilla
AI podcast summaries could be the end of podcasts — or at least of purely informational ones
The experiment proves the value of the hosts' own format: reactive humour and genuine interaction are what listeners come for
